title: The Wild Beasts and the Miracle Year
teaser: In Paris, painters called 'wild beasts' unleash color from reality. In Dresden, students found a bridge to the future. In Bern, a patent clerk rewrites the universe. In St. Petersburg, a massacre ignites revolution. The old certainties shatter simultaneously.

art.label: Art
art.content: At the Salon d'Automne in October, Henri Matisse exhibits Woman with a Hat — a portrait of his wife in blotches of green, pink, and yellow that scandalize Paris. Critic Louis Vauxcelles, seeing a classical sculpture surrounded by these violent canvases, quips: 'Donatello among the wild beasts' — and Fauvism is born. Matisse, André Derain, and Maurice de Vlaminck share a conviction: color need not describe reality; it expresses emotion. Meanwhile in Dresden on June 7th, four architecture students — Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Erich Heckel, Karl Schmidt-Rottluff, and Fritz Bleyl — found Die Brücke (The Bridge), aiming to connect 'all the revolutionary and fermenting elements.' The first avant-garde movements of the twentieth century emerge within months of each other, declaring war on artistic convention.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: In April, Rainer Maria Rilke publishes Das Stunden-Buch (The Book of Hours), three years of mystical poetry written between 1899 and 1903 — a neo-Romantic encounter with God that operates through subjective experience rather than doctrine. Heinrich Mann publishes Professor Unrat, a scathing indictment of Wilhelmine authoritarianism through the downfall of a tyrannical schoolmaster (later filmed as The Blue Angel). In Russia, Maxim Gorky — already the voice of the dispossessed — is arrested for his role in the January uprising. The literary establishment is dividing: Mann's social critique and Gorky's proletarian realism push toward Naturalism's political edge, while Rilke retreats into the interior world that will flower into Modernist subjectivity.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: In Göttingen, Edmund Husserl — whose Logical Investigations (1900–01) launched phenomenology — is refining the method of epoché: bracketing assumptions about external reality to focus on consciousness itself. His students begin forming a dedicated circle. Across the Atlantic, William James lectures on pragmatism at Wellesley — truth as what works in practice, reality as partly constructed through experience. Both challenge the crisis of positivism: the sense that scientific objectivity cannot capture what matters most. The nineteenth century trusted that physics explained the world; 1905 will prove physics didn't even understand space and time.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On January 22nd (January 9th Old Style), a peaceful procession of workers led by Father Georgy Gapon marches to the Winter Palace in St. Petersburg, petitioning Tsar Nicholas II for reforms. Imperial guards open fire, killing hundreds — Bloody Sunday ignites the Russian Revolution of 1905. Strikes paralyze the empire; workers' councils (soviets) form spontaneously. By October, a general strike forces the Tsar to issue the October Manifesto, promising civil liberties and an elected Duma. Meanwhile in Bern, a twenty-six-year-old patent clerk named Albert Einstein publishes four papers in Annalen der Physik — on the photoelectric effect (June), Brownian motion (July), special relativity (September), and mass-energy equivalence (E=mc²). An annus mirabilis that remakes physics.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The convergence is the dissolution of stable reference points. Einstein abolishes absolute space and time; the Fauves abolish color's obligation to describe; Husserl brackets the external world to investigate pure consciousness; the Russian workers discover that the Tsar won't protect them. None of these figures influenced each other directly in 1905 — Einstein worked in isolation, Kirchner knew nothing of Matisse, Husserl and James developed parallel critiques. What connects them is the historical condition: the crisis of positivism had undermined confident materialism; the old certainties of church, monarch, and Newtonian physics were all cracking under their own contradictions. The twentieth century begins not in 1900 but here, when artists, scientists, and revolutionaries simultaneously conclude that reality is not what it seemed.
conn.funFact: Gertrude and Leo Stein bought Matisse's Woman with a Hat directly from the Salon scandal for 500 francs — about four months of a Parisian worker's wages. Their apartment became the first salon of Modernism.

title: The Modernist Explosion
teaser: Joyce, Eliot, Woolf, Wittgenstein — in a single year, the old world of art and thought is detonated.

art.label: Art
art.content: The Bauhaus is in full swing under Gropius — Klee, Kandinsky, Moholy-Nagy teaching the radical idea that art, craft, and industry should merge. It's the institutional arm of Constructivism and De Stijl: strip art to pure form, then rebuild the world. Mondrian pushes into geometric abstraction. In Mexico, Rivera begins his first major mural — Mexican Muralism insists art must be public, political, and monumental, not locked in galleries.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: The greatest year in literary Modernism. Joyce's Ulysses (published in Paris, banned in the US/UK) detonates narrative form — the novel as total experiment. Eliot's The Waste Land does the same for poetry: fragments shored against ruins. Woolf's Jacob's Room pioneers stream-of-consciousness. Proust dies in November, In Search of Lost Time unfinished. Rilke completes the Duino Elegies in a single burst. All are responding to WWI's destruction of 19th-century certainties.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: Wittgenstein's Tractatus appears in English — the founding text of logical positivism, arguing philosophy's problems are really problems of language. The Vienna Circle is forming around Schlick, taking Wittgenstein further than he intended. Heidegger lectures at Freiburg, developing existential phenomenology — the opposite pole, insisting that Being, not logic, is philosophy's proper subject. The discipline is splitting into two traditions that still haven't reconciled.

hist.label: History
hist.content: The Soviet Union is formally established — the Bolshevik experiment becomes a state. Mussolini marches on Rome — fascism takes power for the first time. The Ottoman Empire collapses; Turkey becomes a republic under Atatürk. Tutankhamun's tomb is discovered. The world is four years past WWI, and the interwar order is already fracturing between communism, fascism, and liberal democracy — the three-way struggle that will define the century.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: Everything connects through fragmentation. Eliot's Waste Land is literally fragments. Joyce fragments narrative into a dozen styles. The Bauhaus fragments art into geometry. Wittgenstein fragments language into logical atoms. Why? Because the war fragmented everything — empires, bodies, certainties. Modernism isn't a style; it's the art of a shattered world trying to reassemble itself. Proust dies trying to capture all of time; Wittgenstein insists we stay silent about what we can't capture. Two responses to the same impossibility.
conn.funFact: Ezra Pound edited The Waste Land so ruthlessly he cut it nearly in half. The original draft, found in 1968, suggests Pound may have been the greatest editor in literary history.

title: The Year the World Caught Fire
teaser: Prague Spring. Paris barricades. Prague tanks. MLK and RFK assassinated. Tet Offensive. The old order fractures everywhere at once.

art.label: Art
art.content: Art ruptures in every direction. Conceptual Art crystallises with the formation of the Art & Language group and Lawrence Weiner's declaration that the idea alone is the work — execution optional. Land Art debuts with the "Earthworks" exhibition at Dwan Gallery, where Robert Smithson and Michael Heizer drag art out of galleries into desert landscapes. In June, Valerie Solanas shoots Andy Warhol; the Pope of Pop survives but withdraws from filmmaking. Meanwhile, 2001: A Space Odyssey premieres in April — Kubrick's monolith stands as enigmatic monument to an unknowable future. Art abandons objects for concepts, galleries for earth, screen for mind.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: New Journalism captures the decade's acid-soaked energy: Tom Wolfe's The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test follows Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters into psychedelic consciousness. Norman Mailer's The Armies of the Night makes the author both participant and chronicler of the Pentagon march. Philip K. Dick's Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? asks what humanity means in a mechanised world. From the USSR, Solzhenitsyn's In the First Circle smuggles out witness to the Gulag. And García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude, published the year before in Spanish, spreads like wildfire — magical realism offers escape and reflection alike.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: Ideas arm the barricades. Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man (1964) becomes the bible of the New Left, diagnosing how consumer capitalism absorbs all opposition. Guy Debord's Society of the Spectacle (1967) provides the theoretical framework — modern life has become representation of life, image consuming reality. Slogans appear on Paris walls: "Sous les pavés, la plage!" — under the cobblestones, the beach. Meanwhile, Derrida delivers his lecture on différance in January, deconstruction quietly dismantling the certainties that the streets are loudly rejecting. Post-structuralism and street revolution share a target: inherited structures that pretend to be nature.

hist.label: History
hist.content: The year shatters the postwar consensus. In January, the Tet Offensive stuns America — victory in Vietnam, long promised, suddenly vanishes. In April, Martin Luther King Jr. is assassinated in Memphis; Robert Kennedy, announcing the news in Indianapolis, quotes Aeschylus on wisdom through suffering. Two months later, Kennedy himself is shot. In Prague, Dubček's "socialism with a human face" flowers in spring and dies in August under Soviet tanks. In Paris, students occupy the Sorbonne in May; ten million workers join them; de Gaulle nearly falls. In Chicago, police riot at the Democratic convention. In Mexico City, students are massacred days before the Olympics. Everywhere, youth confronts power — and power fights back.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: What connects student barricades in Paris to tanks in Prague to assassinations in America? The same rupture: the postwar settlement cracking open. Debord's spectacle critique explains why television brought Tet's carnage into living rooms and broke the war consensus. Marcuse's "Great Refusal" gives vocabulary to Paris students and Berkeley activists alike. Derrida's deconstruction and the Situationists' détournement share a method — taking apart received structures to reveal what they conceal. Even 2001's enigmatic monolith mirrors the moment: something is coming that cannot be named, only experienced. The old authorities — state, party, church, academy — lose their spell simultaneously across cultures. Not coincidence: connection through circuits of books, films, radio, and the first global generation raised on television.
conn.funFact: When Robert Kennedy announced King's assassination to a crowd in Indianapolis, he improvised a speech quoting Aeschylus from memory — the only major American city with a scheduled rally that night that did not riot.

title: The Year of Liberty and Reason
teaser: In a single year, Adam Smith invents economics, Gibbon begins Rome's autopsy, Paine ignites revolution, and David Hume — the great skeptic — faces death with serene composure. Three books and one Declaration reshape the world.

art.label: Art
art.content: The Royal Academy in London, founded just eight years earlier, is in full flourish. Joshua Reynolds, its president, continues his mission to elevate British painting to the 'Grand Style' — history painting in the classical manner. His Discourses lectures shape a generation. In France, the late Rococo gives way to austere intimacy: Fragonard's A Young Girl Reading (c. 1776) glows with quiet domestic light, Enlightenment rationality domesticated. Meanwhile Benjamin West paints classical allegory in Philadelphia's shadow. Art hasn't yet absorbed the Revolution — that will come with David's Neoclassicism — but the visual language of republican virtue is being prepared.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: Two of history's most consequential books appear within weeks. On 9 March, Adam Smith publishes An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations — seventeen years in the making, the founding text of classical economics. Division of labour, free markets, the 'invisible hand': the vocabulary of capitalism is born. In February, Edward Gibbon releases Volume I of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, beginning a six-volume autopsy of civilisational collapse. His controversial thesis — that Christianity contributed to Rome's decline — scandalises the pious. Both books share a method: empirical observation over dogma, systematic analysis over tradition.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: On 25 August, David Hume dies in Edinburgh, having written his autobiography during his final illness with detached irony. The great empiricist and skeptic faces death with such cheerful composure that it troubles believers more than his philosophy ever did. His friend Adam Smith publishes an account of his peaceful end that causes scandal — how dare a man die well without religion? Meanwhile in Scotland, Thomas Reid's Common Sense philosophy rises as a counterweight to Humean skepticism, arguing for self-evident first principles. Across the Atlantic, Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense (January 1776) turns philosophical abstraction into revolutionary firepower: fifty-six pages that sell 500,000 copies and make independence thinkable.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On 4 July, the Second Continental Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence. Jefferson's prose crystallises Enlightenment philosophy into political action: 'We hold these truths to be self-evident.' The American Revolution, underway since 1775, now has its manifesto. Across the Atlantic, Britain loses not just colonies but assumptions: that empire is natural, that monarchy is given, that authority flows downward. The Declaration's influence will spread — to France in 1789, to Latin America, to every subsequent revolution claiming natural rights. But in 1776, the outcome is uncertain: Washington's army is ragged, and Britain is the world's greatest military power.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The connections are personal and documented. Adam Smith and David Hume were close friends for decades; Smith visited Hume on his deathbed and later published a controversial letter describing his serene death. Both were central figures of the Scottish Enlightenment, which also influenced Thomas Reid. Hume had earlier read and critiqued Smith's economic writings in draft. Gibbon, though English, moved in the same intellectual circles and shared the empiricist method — applying Humean skepticism to historical sources. Thomas Paine drew on Scottish Common Sense philosophy to make revolutionary arguments accessible. Jefferson knew Smith's work and corresponded with both Scottish and French Enlightenment figures. 1776 marks the moment when Enlightenment philosophy becomes political fact.
conn.funFact: Adam Smith's description of Hume's cheerful death so outraged the religious establishment that Smith received more hate mail for it than for any argument in The Wealth of Nations.

title: Spain — The Year Three Worlds Ended
teaser: Granada falls, ending eight centuries of Islamic Spain. The Alhambra Decree expels the Jews. Columbus sails west. In a single year, the convivencia dies, the Sephardic diaspora begins, and a new age of empire opens.

art.label: Art
art.content: The Hispano-Flemish style dominates Castilian painting — a fusion of Northern European oil technique with Spanish devotional intensity. Pedro Berruguete, recently returned from Urbino, brings Italian perspective to Spanish altarpieces; his Saint Dominic Presiding over an Auto-da-fe (c. 1495) will become an unintentional icon of the Inquisition's reach. Fernando Gallego produces austere Castilian masterpieces marked by angular drapery and psychological severity. Meanwhile, the Alhambra itself — the jewel of Nasrid art — passes into Christian hands. Its muqarnas ceilings, arabesque stucco, and the serene geometry of the Court of Lions represent the apex of Islamic art in Europe, now frozen in time.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: On August 18th, Antonio de Nebrija publishes the Gramática de la lengua castellana — the first grammar of any modern European vernacular. He presents it to Queen Isabella with a famous justification: "Language has always been the companion of empire." The book codifies Castilian orthography, etymology, and syntax just as Castilian is about to spread across oceans. Meanwhile, the expulsion scatters Sephardic literary culture — Hebrew poetry, philosophical commentary, translations from Arabic — to the Ottoman Empire, Italy, and North Africa, where it will flourish in exile while Spain loses its multilingual heritage.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: In Florence, Lorenzo de' Medici dies on April 8th, and with him the golden age of Neoplatonic humanism. The Platonic Academy he had patronized — Ficino, Poliziano, and the young Pico della Mirandola — loses its anchor. Pico's Oration on the Dignity of Man (1486) had declared humanity infinitely perfectible; now his patron is dead, and Pico himself turns increasingly to Savonarola's apocalypticism. Meanwhile in Spain, the Inquisition's logic of limpieza de sangre (blood purity) marks a philosophical rupture: ancestry replaces faith as the measure of orthodoxy, creating Europe's first racial ideology.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On January 2nd, Boabdil surrenders Granada to Ferdinand and Isabella, ending the Reconquista after 781 years. On March 31st, the Alhambra Decree orders all Jews to convert or leave by July 31st — some 40,000–200,000 depart, beginning the Sephardic diaspora. On August 3rd, Columbus sails from Palos with three ships; on October 12th he lands in the Bahamas, believing he has reached Asia. On August 11th, Rodrigo Borgia becomes Pope Alexander VI. Four epochal events in one year: medieval Iberia ends, a diaspora scatters, a hemisphere opens, and the most corrupt pope takes the throne.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The connections are not metaphorical — they are administrative. Columbus watched Granada's surrender; his expedition was authorized in the same palace, Santa Fe, where the surrender terms were negotiated. The expulsion of the Jews and the voyage to the Indies were both funded by confiscated Jewish and Moorish property. Luis de Santángel, a converso financier, personally underwrote Columbus's voyage. Nebrija's grammar and Columbus's log share a premise: Castilian as the language of expanding dominion. The year 1492 isn't a coincidence of dates — it's a single imperial project.
conn.funFact: Columbus's departure from Palos on August 3rd coincided with the final deadline for Jewish expulsion. The harbor was reportedly clogged with refugee ships.

title: The Year Christendom Split
teaser: In Rome and Avignon, two popes excommunicate each other. In Florence, wool carders seize the government. In Padua, Altichiero paints crowds at the cross. Everywhere, the old certainties crack.

art.label: Art
art.content: In Padua, Altichiero da Zevio completes his monumental Crucifixion fresco in the Chapel of San Giacomo at the Basilica di Sant'Antonio. The work represents the final flowering of Trecento naturalism — Giotto's revolution absorbed and extended. Altichiero fills his Crucifixion with over a hundred figures: Roman soldiers, grieving disciples, fainting women, indifferent bystanders. Contemporary portraits appear throughout — Petrarch's face haunts the crowd, King Louis I of Hungary appears in council scenes. The space is deep, the architecture convincing, the emotion individualized. This is painting on the cusp: still Gothic in its gold grounds and pointed arches, already proto-Renaissance in its psychological realism. Altichiero's patrons, the Lupi di Soragna family, commissioned the chapel as a statement of dynastic power in turbulent times.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: In England, William Langland is revising his allegorical masterpiece Piers Plowman — the B-text, composed between 1377 and 1379, transforms his visionary poem into a searing critique of late medieval society. Written in alliterative Middle English, it follows the dreamer Will through corrupted fields, plowmen who cannot find truth, and a Church that has lost its way. Langland writes for common readers in their own tongue. Meanwhile, Catherine of Siena — mystic, diplomat, future Doctor of the Church — has just completed her Dialogue of Divine Providence, dictated in ecstatic visions between 1377 and 1378. She writes in Tuscan vernacular, not Latin, insisting that God speaks through laypeople too. Two vernaculars, two visions, both demanding reform.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: Catherine of Siena embodies a new kind of philosophical authority: the mystical theologian who bypasses clerical mediation to claim direct conversation with God. Her Dialogue presents Christ as a bridge between human and divine — but the bridge is accessible to anyone who seeks it, not controlled by institutional gatekeepers. In England, John Wycliffe pushes this logic further. His De civili dominio (1376-1378) argues that a Church fallen into sin has no right to property, that Scripture alone holds authority, that the papacy itself lacks biblical warrant. Pope Gregory XI condemns nineteen of Wycliffe's propositions in 1377, but powerful nobles protect him. The philosophical ground is shifting: nominalism has severed universals from particulars, and now authority itself seems unmoored from any stable foundation.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On 8 April 1378, a Roman mob surrounds the papal conclave, demanding an Italian pope. The cardinals, terrified, elect Bartolomeo Prignano as Urban VI. Within months, his abrasive reformism alienates the French cardinals. On 20 September 1378, they meet at Fondi and elect Robert of Geneva as Clement VII, who establishes his court at Avignon. The Western Schism begins: two popes, each excommunicating the other's followers, Europe splitting along political lines. In Florence that July, something equally unprecedented: the Ciompi Revolt. Wool carders and unskilled laborers — the popolo minuto without guild representation — storm the Palazzo Vecchio. Michele di Lando, a wool carder, becomes Gonfaloniere of Justice. Three new guilds are created. For six weeks, Florence has a workers' government.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The threads converge in a single question: who holds legitimate authority? In Rome, the cardinals say their first election was coerced — authority requires free consent. In Avignon, Clement VII says the office matters more than the man. Catherine of Siena rushes to Rome to defend Urban VI, writing furious letters calling Clement's cardinals 'incarnate demons'. Wycliffe uses the schism to argue that the papacy itself is illegitimate. In Florence, the Ciompi ask why only guildsmen can govern — why not those who actually work the wool? Altichiero's Crucifixion shows us the other side of crisis: a crowd at the foot of the cross, each face distinct, each responding differently to the same event. There is no single authorized reaction. The center cannot hold because people have stopped believing it was ever the center.
conn.funFact: Catherine of Siena couldn't write until age thirty. She dictated her Dialogue to secretaries while in ecstatic trances, eyes fixed on nothing visible, speaking as if taking God's dictation.

title: Paris — The Terror and the Tyger
teaser: Robespierre invents a new god while the guillotine works overtime. In London, Blake asks who made the Tyger. In a Paris prison, Condorcet writes his last testament to human progress — then dies. Reason devours its children.

art.label: Art
art.content: Jacques-Louis David, the Revolution's official painter, orchestrates the Festival of the Supreme Being on June 8 — a vast spectacle at the Champ-de-Mars with artificial mountains, choirs, and Robespierre descending like a pontiff. But by Thermidor, David is imprisoned. His 1794 Self-Portrait, painted in his cell, shows a different man: the confident neoclassicist now gazes with uncertainty, brush in hand, as if unsure what art means after the Terror. Meanwhile in England, William Blake publishes Europe a Prophecy with its stunning frontispiece The Ancient of Days — Urizen (reason) crouched in a circle of light, compass in hand, measuring the void. Where David's neoclassicism served power, Blake's visionary Romanticism questions whether the creator-god is tyrant or liberator.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: Blake's Songs of Experience appears in 1794, containing the most famous question in English poetry: 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright / In the forests of the night / What immortal hand or eye / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?' The poem interrogates creation itself — is the same god who made the gentle lamb also responsible for predatory violence? In Paris, André Chénier, a poet who supported the Revolution then denounced its excesses, smuggles verses out of Saint-Lazare prison in his laundry. His Iambes burn with fury against the Terror: 'Like a flock of bleating sheep / Soissons, Meaux, Versailles... all to the scaffold.' He is executed on July 25, three days before Robespierre falls. Published posthumously in 1819, his poetry will inspire the Romantics.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: In hiding from the Jacobins, Condorcet writes his Sketch for a Historical Picture of the Progress of the Human Mind — the supreme statement of Enlightenment optimism, arguing that humanity advances inevitably toward reason, equality, and happiness through the accumulation of knowledge. He dies in prison in March, possibly by suicide, his utopian vision a stark contrast to the guillotines outside. Meanwhile, Robespierre delivers his terrifying synthesis: 'If the basis of popular government in peacetime is virtue, the basis during revolution is both virtue and terror.' The Cult of the Supreme Being — Robespierre's attempt to replace Christianity with civic deism — recognises a creator god and the immortality of the soul. Enlightenment reason has become a new religion, complete with festivals, priests, and executions for heretics.

hist.label: History
hist.content: The year 1794 marks both the apex and collapse of the Reign of Terror. The Law of 22 Prairial (June 10) accelerates executions by eliminating defence counsel and allowing only acquittal or death. In the six weeks that follow — the Great Terror — over 1,300 are guillotined in Paris alone. On 9 Thermidor (July 27), the Convention turns on Robespierre himself; he is executed the next day. The Thermidorian Reaction begins: radical Jacobins are purged, the Terror ends, and the Revolution enters a more conservative phase. France has lost some 17,000 to the guillotine, countless more to civil war. The question — can revolution achieve virtue through violence? — will haunt European politics for two centuries.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: Blake's Tyger and Robespierre's Supreme Being both confront the same problem: what kind of creator makes a world of predation and violence? Blake answers with a question; Robespierre answers with a festival. Both reject orthodox Christianity — Blake seeing it as priestcraft, Robespierre seeing it as counter-revolutionary — but Blake distrusts all systems that claim to measure the infinite with compasses. His Urizen is reason-as-tyrant, the very force the Jacobins worship. Condorcet's Sketch, meanwhile, is the last gasp of a faith that the Terror has already refuted: humanity progressing through reason toward perfection, even as reason's disciples send each other to the scaffold. The Romantics who inherit this moment — Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron — will carry the wound: reason promised liberation, but delivered terror.
conn.funFact: André Chénier's final poem, La Jeune Captive, was written for fellow prisoner Aimée de Coigny. She survived Thermidor; he did not. The poem's refrain — 'I do not want to die yet' — was read at his execution.

title: The Year of Departures
teaser: Delacroix exhibits Liberty amid gunsmoke. Hugo saves a cathedral with ink. Darwin sails toward a theory that will reshape creation. Hegel dies as cholera sweeps Europe. In Virginia, Nat Turner teaches America that slavery's peace is a lie. The old world is leaving — what comes next is uncharted.

art.label: Art
art.content: At the Salon of 1831, Eugène Delacroix exhibits Liberty Leading the People — a bare-breasted Marianne striding over corpses, tricolour in hand, leading a motley army of workers, bourgeois, and street urchins through the gunsmoke of the July Revolution. This is French Romanticism made political: where Neoclassicism demanded noble restraint, Delacroix gives us chaos, passion, real bodies. King Louis-Philippe buys the painting — then hides it. Too incendiary for the regime it celebrates. The work earns Delacroix the Legion of Honor but won't be publicly displayed again until 1848, when revolution returns. Meanwhile, across the Channel, John Constable is painting the English countryside with scientific precision, his cloud studies informed by the new meteorology. Romantic nature worship and empirical observation are learning to coexist.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: On March 16th, Victor Hugo publishes Notre-Dame de Paris. The real protagonist isn't Quasimodo — it's the cathedral itself, which Hugo describes in loving architectural detail precisely because it was being neglected, vandalized, even slated for demolition. The novel is a polemic disguised as romance: Hugo invents gothic revival literature to save gothic architecture. He succeeds — the novel's popularity sparks a national movement for restoration. In Russia, Pushkin completes the final chapters of Eugene Onegin, the 'novel in verse' that invents modern Russian literature. Its ironic narrator, formal innovation, and psychological ambiguity make it the bridge between Romanticism and Realism. Stendhal's Le Rouge et le Noir, published the previous year, is finding readers — its cold psychological dissection of ambition pointing toward the novels to come.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: On November 14th, Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel dies in Berlin, likely of cholera. He is sixty-one, at the height of his fame, having served as university rector just the year before. His death marks the end of German Idealism's greatest system — the dialectical philosophy of Spirit realizing itself through history, thesis meeting antithesis in ever-higher synthesis. But Hegel's students are already dividing into warring camps. The Right Hegelians will use his philosophy to justify the Prussian state; the Young Hegelians — including a young Karl Marx, who won't arrive in Berlin until 1836 — will turn it into a weapon against religion, hierarchy, and eventually capitalism itself. The master is dead; the interpretation wars begin.

hist.label: History
hist.content: In August, the enslaved preacher Nat Turner leads the deadliest slave rebellion in American history. Interpreting a solar eclipse as divine command, Turner and some seventy followers kill fifty-five white men, women, and children in Southampton County, Virginia, before being suppressed. The white backlash is savage: over a hundred Black people, most uninvolved, are murdered in retaliation. Turner evades capture for two months, then is hanged on November 11th. The South responds with brutal new slave codes restricting education, assembly, even worship. In Europe, Belgium declares independence from the Netherlands; Leopold I becomes the first King of the Belgians. And on December 27th, a twenty-two-year-old naturalist named Charles Darwin sails from Plymouth aboard HMS Beagle — a five-year voyage that will give him the observations for a theory that will make Hegel's Spirit obsolete.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The departures are literal and metaphorical. Hegel dies; Darwin embarks. One system of explaining everything (Spirit, dialectic, teleology) passes; another (evolution, natural selection, material mechanism) is about to be born — though Darwin won't publish On the Origin of Species for nearly three decades. Hugo and Delacroix both respond to the July Revolution — Hugo by looking backward to medieval France, Delacroix by painting the present in mythological terms. Both are Romantics reaching for something larger than bourgeois reality: the sacred architecture of the past, the goddess of liberty in the streets. Turner's rebellion reveals what rational systems obscure — that millions live in bondage, that 'progress' is unevenly distributed, that Enlightenment ideals of freedom can coexist with chattel slavery. The year 1831 is a hinge: Romanticism at its peak, Realism stirring, and aboard the Beagle, the seeds of a materialism that will reshape the nineteenth century.
conn.funFact: Louis-Philippe bought Liberty Leading the People with state funds — then hid it from public view for seventeen years. A revolution made safe for museums was still too dangerous for the walls.

title: Verdun — The Birth of Nations
teaser: Three brothers divide an empire and unknowingly create Europe. In the ashes of Carolingian unity, the first words of French and German are spoken — and a thousand years of conflict begins.

art.label: Art
art.content: The Court School of Charles the Bald flourishes even as the empire fractures. In 845, the Vivian Bible (First Bible of Charles the Bald) will emerge from the scriptorium at Tours — a masterpiece of Carolingian illumination featuring full-page miniatures of Jerome, David, and Charles himself receiving the book. The dedication image shows the king enthroned, surrounded by courtiers, establishing visual conventions of sacred kingship that will echo through medieval art. Meanwhile, the Utrecht Psalter, completed around 820-840 at Hautvillers near Reims, represents the most revolutionary manuscript of the era: 166 pen-and-ink drawings that visualise the psalms with nervous, dynamic energy unprecedented in Western art — a style that will influence English illumination for centuries.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: The Oaths of Strasbourg, sworn in February 842, preserve the earliest surviving texts in what would become French and German. Louis the German swears in lingua romana (Old French) so Charles's troops can understand; Charles swears in lingua teudisca (Old High German) for Louis's army. The chronicler Nithard — Charlemagne's grandson — records these oaths in his Historiae, writing as both participant and historian. His account, completed before his death in 844, provides the only eyewitness narrative of the civil war and preserves these linguistic monuments. The deliberate use of vernacular for a political treaty marks a revolutionary moment: Latin's monopoly on formal discourse begins to crack.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: At Charles the Bald's court, John Scottus Eriugena arrives around 845 to lead the Palace School — the most original philosopher between Boethius and Anselm. His mastery of Greek (rare in the Latin West) allows him to translate Pseudo-Dionysius and develop a sophisticated Neoplatonism that will later be condemned as pantheistic. Meanwhile, Paschasius Radbertus at Corbie presents his treatise De Corpore et Sanguine Domini to Charles in 844 — the first systematic argument for what will become transubstantiation. His claim that the consecrated bread is Christ's historical body sparks the Carolingian Eucharist controversy, with Ratramnus offering a more symbolic interpretation. The debate prefigures conflicts that will split Western Christianity seven centuries later.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On August 10, 843, at Verdun, Lothair I, Louis the German, and Charles the Bald sign the treaty that ends three years of civil war. The carnage had peaked at the Battle of Fontenoy (June 841), where perhaps 40,000 Franks slaughtered each other — contemporaries called it unprecedented. The treaty divides the Carolingian Empire into three: West Francia (future France) for Charles, East Francia (future Germany) for Louis, and Middle Francia — a fragile corridor from the North Sea to Rome — for Lothair, who keeps the imperial title. Middle Francia will prove ungovernable; its remnants (Lotharingia, Alsace-Lorraine) will be fought over for a millennium.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The Oaths of Strasbourg reveal what the Treaty of Verdun formalises: Charlemagne's empire has become linguistically as well as politically divided. When kings must translate for each other's armies, the fiction of Frankish unity is dead. Yet fragmentation paradoxically stimulates culture: Charles the Bald, competing for legitimacy, becomes the greatest art patron of the age. The Vivian Bible's dedication image — the king as sacred recipient of God's word — invents visual propaganda that will serve monarchs for eight centuries. Eriugena's Greek translations preserve Neoplatonic theology that scholastics will rediscover. And the partition itself creates the template of European history: France and Germany as distinct entities, with the lands between them (Belgium, Netherlands, Alsace-Lorraine, Italy) as eternal battlegrounds.
conn.funFact: The Oaths of Strasbourg, sworn to unite two brothers against a third, are now studied not for their politics but as linguistic monuments — the birth certificates of the French and German languages.

title: Christendom's Triple Frontier
teaser: A Frankish hammer stops the Umayyad advance at Tours. A Byzantine emperor smashes icons. A Northumbrian monk completes the first history of England. Three frontiers of Christendom — military, theological, intellectual — defended in a single generation.

art.label: Art
art.content: The Lindisfarne Gospels (c. 715-720) represent the zenith of Insular art — that fusion of Celtic spirals, Germanic animal interlace, and Mediterranean tradition forged in the monasteries of Britain and Ireland. Created by Bishop Eadfrith on Holy Island, the manuscript uses techniques borrowed from elite metalwork: the famous carpet pages dissolve representation into abstract infinity, while the evangelist portraits adapt Byzantine models into something wholly original. This is devotional art that exceeds its sources — a visual theology arguing that beauty itself can be prayer. Meanwhile in Constantinople, Emperor Leo III orders icons removed from churches, beginning the Iconoclast Controversy that will convulse Byzantine art for over a century.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: In 731, Bede completes his Ecclesiastical History of the English People at the monastery of Jarrow — the first comprehensive history of England and one of the finest works of medieval historiography. Bede pioneers techniques still used today: he dates events by the Anno Domini system, cites his sources, and distinguishes between eyewitness testimony and tradition. His careful prose transforms the chaotic conversion of Anglo-Saxon kingdoms into a coherent narrative of providence. The work will spread across Europe within a generation, establishing Bede as 'the Father of English History' and making Northumbria a beacon of Latin learning at the edge of the known world.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: From the safety of the Mar Saba monastery in Muslim-controlled Palestine, John of Damascus composes his Three Treatises on the Divine Images (c. 726-730) — the foundational defence of icon veneration. His argument is philosophical and Christological: because God became visible flesh in Christ, matter itself can convey the sacred. The distinction between latria (worship owed to God alone) and proskynesis (veneration offered to saints and images) will shape Orthodox and Catholic theology permanently. John writes beyond the Emperor's reach — the first major theologian to benefit from Islam's relative tolerance of Christian intellectual life.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On 10 October 732, Charles Martel and his Frankish infantry halt the Umayyad advance at Tours (or Poitiers) — the deepest Islamic penetration into Western Europe. The Umayyad commander Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi dies in battle; his army retreats to Al-Andalus. Historians debate whether the caliphate ever intended permanent northern conquest, but the consequences were real: Charles emerges as Europe's dominant warlord, founding the dynasty that will produce Charlemagne. The same decade sees the Umayyad Caliphate at its territorial peak — from Spain to the Indus — and approaching the internal crisis that will shatter it in 750.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: Christendom is fighting on three frontiers simultaneously — and winning. Charles defends the military frontier against Islamic expansion. John of Damascus defends the theological frontier against imperial iconoclasm, preserving the visual vocabulary of faith. Bede defends the intellectual frontier, proving that the converted 'barbarians' of Britain can produce scholarship rivalling anything from Rome's golden age. The Lindisfarne Gospels embody this confidence: art so accomplished it needs no justification, created at what should be civilisation's edge. When Viking raiders destroy Lindisfarne in 793, this generation's achievement will have already seeded the Carolingian Renaissance — Alcuin of York, trained in Bede's Northumbria, will carry the learning to Charlemagne's court.
conn.funFact: John of Damascus wrote his defence of icons while living under Muslim rule — safe from the Christian emperor who wanted to destroy them. The irony was not lost on his contemporaries.

title: Harpers Ferry & Down — Origins
teaser: Darwin publishes the theory that will reshape everything. John Brown raids an arsenal and reshapes America. Mill defends liberty against the majority. In Russia, Oblomov refuses to get out of bed. The old certainties are dissolving — into struggle.

art.label: Art
art.content: In Italy, Francesco Hayez paints The Kiss — a couple locked in passionate embrace against a medieval backdrop. The painting becomes an icon of the Risorgimento: romantic nationalism as visual allegory, the man's departure hinting at the volunteers leaving to fight Austria. In America, Frederic Church's The Heart of the Andes draws twelve thousand paying visitors in New York — panoramic Luminism rendering nature as revelation, five by ten feet of Ecuadorian mountains suffused with transcendent light. The year also sees Édouard Manet's The Absinthe Drinker rejected by the Salon — a modern Parisian subject painted with bold simplification. The gatekeepers don't know it yet, but modernism is knocking.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: Charles Dickens launches A Tale of Two Cities in his new magazine, All the Year Round — revolution as resurrection, the Terror as moral crucible. George Eliot's Adam Bede establishes her as the master of English psychological realism: rural England rendered with sociological precision and moral depth. In Russia, Ivan Goncharov publishes Oblomov — a nobleman who barely leaves his bed, the superfluous man as social diagnosis. And Edward FitzGerald quietly releases his Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, initially ignored but destined to become the Victorian era's favorite exotic pessimism: "The Moving Finger writes; and, having writ, Moves on."

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: On November 24th, Charles Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species. The first edition of 1,250 copies sells out immediately. Species are not fixed creations but mutable descendants of common ancestors, shaped by natural selection — the struggle for existence favoring variations that aid survival. It's the most important scientific work since Newton, and it will detonate through theology, ethics, and social theory for generations. The same year, John Stuart Mill publishes On Liberty, written with his late wife Harriet Taylor — the foundational text of modern liberalism. Against the tyranny of the majority, Mill defends the absolute sovereignty of the individual over their own body and mind: "Over himself, his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign."

hist.label: History
hist.content: On October 16th, the abolitionist John Brown leads twenty-one men in a raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia — intending to spark a slave insurrection. The raid fails; Brown is captured by a young Robert E. Lee, tried for treason, and hanged on December 2nd. But his composure at trial galvanizes Northern abolitionists — Emerson calls him a saint, Thoreau a martyr. The South sees terrorism; the North, prophecy. Meanwhile, at Solferino in June, French and Piedmontese forces defeat Austria in the bloodiest battle since Waterloo — forty thousand casualties in a single day. A Swiss businessman named Henry Dunant witnesses the aftermath and will found the Red Cross.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: Darwin and John Brown share more than a year. Both challenge assumptions about what can change — species, societies — and both frame change as struggle. Darwin's 'struggle for existence' will be misappropriated by Social Darwinists to justify exactly the hierarchies Brown died opposing. Mill's defense of individual liberty and experiment implicitly supports both: scientific heterodoxy and moral dissent. Even Oblomov connects — Goncharov's paralyzed nobleman is what Russia's intelligentsia feared they were becoming: all thought, no action. Dunant at Solferino and Brown at Harpers Ferry both confront massive violence and refuse to look away; one founds humanitarianism, the other martyrdom. The year 1859 is about what it costs to act on what you see.
conn.funFact: Darwin delayed publishing for twenty years, fearing the implications. What forced his hand? In 1858, Alfred Russel Wallace independently arrived at the same theory and wrote to Darwin announcing his intention to publish. Darwin rushed the book into print. Evolution nearly had two fathers.

title: Amsterdam — The Year of Thinking Dangerously
teaser: Spinoza publishes anonymously and is banned. Pascal's unfinished defense of faith appears from the grave. Molière mocks the bourgeoisie while Vermeer paints its quiet devotion. A princess negotiates a secret treaty — and dies weeks later. The Dutch Golden Age reaches its zenith before the fall.

art.label: Art
art.content: Johannes Vermeer completes The Lacemaker around 1669–1670 — at just 24 by 21 centimeters, his smallest canvas transforms domestic labour into luminous meditation. A young woman bends over her bobbins, utterly absorbed; the threads in the foreground blur as if seen through a lens, while her face and hands hold perfect focus. Vermeer's use of the camera obscura is evident in these optical effects that no human eye produces unaided. In the same years he paints Allegory of the Catholic Faith, a rare departure into history painting: a woman personifying Faith rests her foot on a globe, a crushed serpent beneath it. Vermeer, a Catholic convert in Protestant Holland, paints what cannot be publicly celebrated — faith practiced in the 'hidden churches' (schuilkerken) where Mass was permitted but not flaunted. Meanwhile, Rembrandt has been dead since October 1669, bankrupt and largely forgotten. The Dutch Golden Age continues without its greatest master, its merchant patrons preferring Vermeer's serene interiors to Rembrandt's psychological depths.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: Two posthumous works reshape French thought. Blaise Pascal's Pensées appears in print, eight years after his death — fragments of an unfinished apology for Christianity, arranged by the Port-Royal editors with cautious cuts. Pascal's wager emerges: even if God's existence is uncertain, the infinite reward for belief outweighs the finite cost. "The heart has its reasons which reason knows not." Simultaneously, Molière premieres Le Bourgeois gentilhomme at Chambord for Louis XIV — a comedy-ballet skewering Monsieur Jourdain, who discovers he has been speaking prose all his life. Molière's satire of social climbing delights the aristocrats whose power depends on keeping merchants in their place. In Paris, Jean Racine's Bérénice premieres at the Hôtel de Bourgogne — a tragedy of renunciation where love yields to duty, based on the Roman emperor Titus who sent away the queen he adored. In England, John Dryden is appointed Historiographer Royal; Milton's Paradise Regained is licensed, to appear the following year.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: In Amsterdam, Baruch Spinoza publishes Tractatus Theologico-Politicus anonymously, with a false imprint claiming it was printed in Hamburg. The gambit fails: within months, the Dutch Reformed Church condemns it as "forged in hell by a renegade Jew and the devil." Spinoza argues that Scripture must be read historically and critically, not as literal truth; that miracles are impossible because nature is God and cannot contradict itself; and that freedom of thought is essential to a peaceful state. He separates philosophy from theology — reason deals with truth, religion with piety. The Tractatus will be formally banned in 1674, driving his Ethics underground until after his death. Spinoza earns his living grinding lenses for microscopes and telescopes — the instruments that let others see clearly while his books remain veiled. Across the Channel, Cambridge Platonists like Henry More and Ralph Cudworth seek a middle way between Cartesian mechanism and Spinozan monism, defending free will and a universe penetrated by spirit.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On 1 June 1670, the Secret Treaty of Dover is signed between Charles II of England and Louis XIV of France. The public treaty commits England to support France against the Dutch Republic. The secret clauses — known only to five English ministers — commit Charles to convert to Catholicism and restore the faith in England, in exchange for French subsidies and six thousand troops to suppress any rebellion. The treaty is negotiated by Charles's beloved sister Henrietta Anne, Duchess of Orléans, who crosses to Dover for fifteen days of festivities. On 30 June, three weeks after returning to France, she collapses at Saint-Cloud after drinking iced chicory water, crying "I have been poisoned!" She dies within hours at age twenty-six. An autopsy rules natural causes — likely a ruptured appendix — but suspicion falls on her husband's lover, the Chevalier de Lorraine. The Dutch Golden Age stands at its zenith: Amsterdam is the world's richest city, the Dutch East India Company dominates global trade. But 1672 approaches — the Rampjaar, the Disaster Year, when France, England, and German states will attack simultaneously.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The year 1670 stages a collision between public performance and private truth. Spinoza publishes anonymously because stating openly what he believes would destroy him; Pascal's fragments speak from the grave because he died before finishing his argument. Vermeer paints Catholic faith in a country where Catholicism is tolerated but hidden. Charles II signs a treaty promising Catholic restoration while ruling Protestant England. Molière mocks pretension while depending entirely on royal patronage. Racine's Bérénice dramatises the painful gap between private desire and public duty — exactly what Henrietta Anne navigated between her brother and brother-in-law, dying before she could see the consequences. The Dutch Republic permits Spinoza to think freely and then bans what he thinks. The Golden Age generates both Vermeer's quiet mastery and the VOC's global exploitation. Every surface conceals another surface: prose beneath poetry, heresy beneath anonymity, conspiracy beneath diplomacy.
conn.funFact: Spinoza's lens-grinding was more than a modest trade — his optical work was highly regarded. Christiaan Huygens, the greatest physicist in Europe, praised Spinoza's lenses. The philosopher who saw God in nature helped others see the moons of Jupiter and the microorganisms in pond water.

title: Geneva — The Haunted Summer
teaser: Mount Tambora blots out the sun. At a rain-soaked villa on Lake Geneva, teenagers invent Gothic horror. Byron writes an apocalypse poem that wasn't metaphor. Coleridge finally publishes his opium dream. The skies burn red, the crops fail, and Romanticism finds its darkness.

art.label: Art
art.content: J.M.W. Turner begins sketching the volcanic sunsets that will define his later career — the fiery reds and oranges aren't poetic exaggeration but direct observation of Tambora's atmospheric veil. Between 1816 and 1818, he fills a sketchbook with 65 watercolours documenting skies 'dripping with gold and scarlet.' John Constable works in a different mode: his Wivenhoe Park (1816) renders the English countryside with scientific precision, cloud studies informed by the new meteorology. Where Turner dissolves form into light, Constable measures nature empirically — both responses to a Romantic moment that demanded close attention to weather and atmosphere.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: In June, Lord Byron, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Mary Godwin, and Byron's physician John Polidori gather at Villa Diodati on Lake Geneva — trapped indoors by incessant cold rain. Byron proposes a ghost story contest. Mary Godwin, eighteen years old, conceives Frankenstein; Polidori sketches what will become The Vampyre, the first modern vampire fiction. Byron himself writes 'Darkness' — a blank-verse vision of the sun extinguished: 'The bright sun was extinguish'd, and the stars / Did wander darkling in the eternal space.' Not metaphor — description. Meanwhile, Coleridge finally publishes Kubla Khan, the fragment of an opium dream transcribed nineteen years earlier, its 'caverns measureless to man' and 'sunless sea' now eerily resonant.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: Shelley's Hymn to Intellectual Beauty, composed that summer, seeks an alternative to Christian theodicy — how to explain evil without a personal god? The 'unseen Power' that visits 'with inconstant glance / Each human heart and countenance' is secular, impersonal, yet still mysteriously beautiful. Hegel completes his Science of Logic and accepts a chair at Heidelberg, building the dialectical system that will dominate German thought. But the Year Without a Summer poses a question neither idealism nor natural theology can easily answer: what kind of cosmos produces random catastrophe? The theodicy crisis that began with Lisbon's earthquake in 1755 intensifies. Providence looks increasingly like accident.

hist.label: History
hist.content: Mount Tambora's April 1815 eruption — the largest in recorded history — ejects 150 cubic kilometres of ash and sulphur into the stratosphere. By 1816, global temperatures drop 0.4–0.7°C. In New England, frost kills crops in June; snow falls in New York in July. Europe's harvest fails catastrophically — famine stalks Germany, Switzerland, Ireland. Food riots erupt across the continent. In England, the Spa Fields riots (November–December) demand parliamentary reform as ex-soldiers and unemployed workers clash with authorities. Meanwhile, on July 9, the Congress of Tucumán declares Argentine independence from Spain — revolution continues in South America while Europe freezes under volcanic ash.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The climate catastrophe creates the conditions for Romantic darkness. Byron's 'Darkness' is not allegory — he is describing what he sees outside his window in Geneva, where fowls roosted at noon and candles were lit at midday. Mary Shelley's creature, assembled from dead matter and animated by lightning, is a creation myth for a world where nature has become terrifying and unpredictable. Turner's volcanic sunsets turn empirical observation into sublime vision — science and art fused at the moment when both confront a nature that exceeds human control. The Tambora eruption demonstrates what the philosophers couldn't prove: that the cosmos is indifferent to human flourishing. Romanticism's turn toward the dark sublime — Gothic horror, apocalyptic poetry, melancholy landscapes — is partly meteorological.

title: Brussels — The Year of Uncertainty
teaser: Heisenberg shatters determinism. Heidegger asks what it means to exist in time. Proust's final volume recovers lost time. Woolf dissolves narrative into duration. In Brussels, Einstein and Bohr clash over reality itself. Modernity discovers it cannot know everything at once.

art.label: Art
art.content: René Magritte holds his first solo exhibition at Galerie Le Centaure in Brussels, unveiling The Menaced Assassin — Surrealism's deadpan subversion of reality arrives in full force. In Berlin, Fritz Lang's Metropolis premieres: German Expressionism scaled to industrial nightmare, where workers become extensions of machines. Edward Hopper paints Automat — a woman alone in an all-night diner, American Scene realism capturing urban isolation. Meanwhile in Hollywood, The Jazz Singer introduces synchronised dialogue, ending the silent era and inaugurating cinema's technological disruption of art.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: Proust's Le Temps retrouvé appears posthumously — the final volume of In Search of Lost Time reveals that involuntary memory can defeat death itself. Virginia Woolf publishes To the Lighthouse, dissolving plot into duration: the middle section, 'Time Passes,' condenses ten years and the Great War into twenty pages of empty rooms. Kafka's unfinished Amerika is published posthumously by Max Brod. Modernism's obsession with time — Bergson's durée, Joyce's single day — reaches its philosophical climax: literature doesn't describe time, it becomes temporal experience.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: Martin Heidegger publishes Sein und Zeit (Being and Time), the founding text of existential phenomenology. The question: what does it mean to be? His answer: human existence (Dasein) is fundamentally temporal — we are thrown into time, project ourselves toward death, and find authenticity only by confronting our finitude. Simultaneously, Heisenberg formulates the uncertainty principle: position and momentum cannot both be precisely known. At the Fifth Solvay Conference in October, Bohr's Copenhagen interpretation defeats Einstein's determinism. Reality is irreducibly probabilistic. Philosophy and physics converge on the same insight: certainty is impossible.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On May 20th, Charles Lindbergh departs New York in the Spirit of St. Louis; thirty-three hours later he lands in Paris — the first solo transatlantic flight, collapsing continental distance into human scale. In China, Chiang Kai-shek's April purge in Shanghai massacres thousands of Communists, splitting the First United Front and igniting the Chinese Civil War. Mao Zedong's Autumn Harvest Uprising fails; the survivors retreat to the mountains, beginning the rural guerrilla strategy that will eventually win China. The interwar world: technology annihilating space, ideology consuming nations.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The year's obsession is time and uncertainty. Heidegger argues that existence is temporal before it is anything else; Proust demonstrates that memory can recapture time; Woolf shows duration swallowing individual lives; Heisenberg proves that observation disturbs what it measures. These aren't parallel discoveries — they share a common crisis. The nineteenth century's confident positivism is dead; the new physics and the new literature both insist that the observer is entangled with the observed. At Solvay, Einstein protests: 'God does not play dice.' Bohr replies: 'Stop telling God what to do.' The twentieth century's metaphysics is decided by a vote.
conn.funFact: Seventeen of the twenty-nine physicists at the Solvay Conference were or would become Nobel laureates — the photograph is sometimes called 'the most intelligent picture ever taken.'

title: Paris — Art Against Annihilation
teaser: Guernica screams in gray as German bombs pulverize a Basque town. At the Paris Expo, Spanish republicans mount their pavilion of protest while Nazi and Soviet towers face off like armored titans. Gramsci dies in prison, leaving notebooks that explain how power manufactures consent. Hurston and Tolkien publish masterworks the establishment ignores.

art.label: Art
art.content: The Spanish Pavilion at the Paris International Exposition becomes a sanctuary of resistance, housing Picasso's monumental Guernica alongside Joan Miró's The Reaper and Alexander Calder's Mercury Fountain — artists weaponizing beauty against barbarism. Across the esplanade, Albert Speer's German Pavilion and Boris Iofan's Soviet tower face each other like armored giants, their totalitarian aesthetics of heroic scale and idealized bodies revealing the era's competing visions of human destiny. The year's governing image is Guernica's central lightbulb, that harsh electric eye illuminating atrocity — suggesting both the media apparatus that will broadcast future horrors and the persistence of Enlightenment values under assault.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: Zora Neale Hurston publishes Their Eyes Were Watching God, a novel of Black female self-determination that her Harlem Renaissance peers dismiss but posterity will crown as a masterpiece. John Steinbeck's Of Mice and Men appears in February, while J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit in September opens a door to Middle-earth. In Tehran, Sadegh Hedayat writes The Blind Owl, a hallucinatory meditation on alienation that becomes Persian modernism's founding text. Escape and engagement exist in productive tension — Tolkien's dark lords allegorize contemporary anxieties, while Hurston's Janie Crawford discovers that horizons are 'the beginning of everything.'

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: Antonio Gramsci dies in a fascist prison after eleven years of captivity, his Prison Notebooks containing revolutionary concepts of cultural hegemony and the organic intellectual that will reshape Marxist thought. His essential question: how do ruling classes maintain power not through force alone, but through the manufacture of consent? Edmund Husserl, banned from German universities as a Jew, continues his Crisis of European Sciences, diagnosing the spiritual malaise that rational thought alone cannot cure. The logical positivists gather for their last Paris Congress as their dream of purifying language seems increasingly inadequate to a world where 'blood and soil' slogans mobilize millions.

hist.label: History
hist.content: The Spanish Civil War rages as a testing ground for the coming world conflagration. On April 26th, German Condor Legion planes bomb the Basque market town of Guernica — fascism's most brazen demonstration of terror warfare against civilians. The attack kills hundreds and destroys 85% of the town's buildings, providing Picasso his subject within days. Meanwhile, the Great Purge in the Soviet Union reaches its peak as Stalin eliminates perceived enemies. The Paris International Exposition opens in May, a showcase of modernity where democratic, fascist, and communist visions compete for legitimacy through architectural spectacle.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The year crystallizes modernism under siege. While fascism demonstrates that technology can obliterate ancient cities in an afternoon, artists respond by creating works that refuse the consolations of beauty while insisting on art's moral necessity. Guernica offers no heroes, no narrative resolution, no color — only the fragmented testimony of suffering rendered in Cubism's pictorial vocabulary. The bombed town, the dying republic, the imprisoned philosopher, the exiled artist — 1937 assembles the materials for understanding how civilization collapses and how cultural work might resist, record, or imaginatively transcend that collapse.
conn.funFact: Picasso painted Guernica in just 35 days — the same time it took the bombers to transform a medieval town into ruins and rubble.

title: The Year of Scandal and Freedom
teaser: Manet scandalizes Paris. Lincoln redefines America. Renan humanizes Jesus. Modernity announces itself — naked, democratic, godless.

art.label: Art
art.content: The Salon des Refusés opens in May — Napoleon III's response to protests over 2,000 rejected paintings. Visitors crowd in to laugh, but they're witnessing a revolution. Manet's Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe places a naked woman among clothed men in a contemporary setting — not mythology, but modern life. The scandal isn't the nudity; it's the refusal to idealize. In August, Delacroix dies — the last great Romantic master. The baton passes to a new generation that rejects both classical perfection and Romantic emotionalism in favor of direct confrontation with the present. Baudelaire's essay The Painter of Modern Life, published in Le Figaro, provides the manifesto: beauty is now transient, fleeting, contingent.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: Lincoln's Gettysburg Address — 272 words delivered in November — redefines what America means: not a contract between states but a nation conceived in Liberty. It's the most important piece of American political rhetoric ever written. In France, Jules Verne publishes Five Weeks in a Balloon, launching scientific romance as popular literature. Dostoevsky's Winter Notes on Summer Impressions critiques Western materialism; the underground man is gestating. The year marks the rise of literary realism in tension with the emerging symbolism that Baudelaire champions.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: John Stuart Mill publishes Utilitarianism in book form — the definitive statement of consequentialist ethics: actions are right insofar as they promote the greatest happiness for the greatest number. Ernest Renan's Vie de Jésus becomes an instant bestseller and scandal — treating Jesus as a historical figure, a charming Galilean teacher stripped of miracles and divinity. It's biblical criticism for the masses, attacking the supernatural foundations of Christianity. Both Mill and Renan share the same premise: human reason, not revelation, grounds truth. Positivism and secular humanism advance on multiple fronts.

hist.label: History
hist.content: The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect on January 1st — Lincoln transforms the Civil War from preserving the Union to ending slavery. In July, the Battle of Gettysburg turns the war's tide. In Poland, the January Uprising against Russian rule begins — a nationalist insurrection that will be crushed but galvanize Polish identity for generations. In London, the world's first underground railway opens — the Metropolitan Line — modernity burrowing beneath the streets. The year crystallizes the era's great conflict: democratic self-determination versus established order, science versus tradition, freedom versus hierarchy.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: Everything connects through demystification. Manet strips the nude of classical alibi — she stares at the viewer, modern and unashamed. Renan strips Christ of divinity — he becomes a historical figure, however admirable. Lincoln strips America of its founding compromise with slavery — the Constitution is rewritten in blood and rhetoric. Mill strips ethics of divine command — morality becomes calculus. Even the Metropolitan Railway strips travel of its romance — tunneling through the earth by gaslight, passengers become commuters. Modernity is arriving, and its signature gesture is to remove the veil: to show things as they are, not as tradition dressed them.
conn.funFact: When the Salon jury rejected over half of all submitted paintings in 1863, the protests were so loud that Napoleon III personally visited to see what the fuss was about — and ordered the Salon des Refusés created so the public could judge for themselves.

title: The Year of Collapses
teaser: Napoleon III falls at Sedan. Rome falls to Italy. The Pope falls back on infallibility. One empire dies, two nations are born, and Impressionism flees to London.

art.label: Art
art.content: The Franco-Prussian War scatters the nascent Impressionists. Monet flees to London in September 1870 with his wife and infant son, painting The Thames Below Westminster through winter fog — the Thames, not the Seine, becomes Impressionism's first exile landscape. Pissarro arrives the same autumn, painting Sydenham and Crystal Palace while news arrives that Prussian soldiers are using his canvases as butcher's aprons in Louveciennes. Renoir serves in the cavalry; Bazille is killed at Beaune-la-Rolande in November, twenty-eight years old. Meanwhile, in Munich in June, Wagner's Die Walküre premieres against his explicit wishes — King Ludwig II refuses to wait for Bayreuth. The art that will define modernity is being forged in war, exile, and loss.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: Charles Dickens dies on June 9th, leaving The Mystery of Edwin Drood forever unfinished — Victorian literature's last great voice silenced mid-sentence. The same year, Dante Gabriel Rossetti publishes Poems, many of which had been exhumed from his wife Elizabeth Siddal's grave in Highgate Cemetery in October 1869. Rossetti had buried the only manuscript with her in 1862; seven years later, he had her coffin opened. The poems arrived smelling of disinfectant, tangled in hair that legend said had continued growing. In France, Jules Verne publishes Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea — Captain Nemo's submarine Nautilus attacks warships with deliberate ambiguity about which nation's flag they fly, written as war loomed.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: On July 18th, the First Vatican Council defines papal infallibility as dogma — the Pope cannot err when speaking ex cathedra on faith and morals. Exactly two months later, on September 20th, Italian troops breach the walls at Porta Pia and end the Pope's temporal power forever. Pius IX declares himself a prisoner in the Vatican, refusing to acknowledge the Italian state. The paradox is perfect: spiritual authority made absolute at the moment territorial sovereignty vanishes. Meanwhile, the young Nietzsche, twenty-five and already a Basel professor, serves as a medical orderly in the Prussian army, contracts dysentery and diphtheria tending wounded soldiers in cattle cars. He is writing The Birth of Tragedy, dedicated to Wagner.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On September 2nd, Napoleon III surrenders at Sedan with 100,000 troops — the Second Empire collapses in six weeks of war. The Third Republic is declared on September 4th; Empress Eugénie flees to England. By September 19th, Paris is besieged; it will hold for four months, its inhabitants eating zoo animals and rats. On September 20th, Bersaglieri troops breach the Aurelian Walls at Porta Pia — Rome falls, Italian unification completes, the Pope's thousand-year temporal dominion ends. In January 1871, the German Empire will be proclaimed at Versailles. Three states die (Second Empire, Papal States, German Confederation); three are born (Third Republic, Kingdom of Italy with Rome, German Empire). The map of Europe is rewritten in eight months.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: Everything connects through collapse as creation. The Vatican Council's timing was no accident — Pius IX convened it partly to rally support against Italian encroachment, then found himself defining absolute spiritual authority as his temporal realm contracted to a single palace. Monet and Pissarro's London exile wasn't merely escape; their dealer Durand-Ruel, also in London, would become Impressionism's crucial patron, the commercial infrastructure created by political catastrophe. Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy, germinating amid dysentery and dying soldiers, argues that Greek tragedy emerged from Dionysian chaos — destruction enabling creation. Wagner's Walküre, forced into premiere against his will by a king already showing signs of the madness that would kill him, begins the opera cycle that reimagines Germany's mythology just as Germany militarily remakes itself.
conn.funFact: During the Siege of Paris, Castor and Pollux — the elephants of the Jardin des Plantes — were butchered and sold to wealthy restaurants. The trunk reportedly fetched 45 francs per pound. The zoo's big cats went uneaten; no one wanted to buy predators.

title: The Year of Codes
teaser: Stalin dies. Godot never arrives. Watson and Crick crack life's alphabet. Wittgenstein rewrites philosophy from the grave. In Paris, two tramps wait for meaning. In Washington, the Rosenbergs go to the chair. Codes everywhere — genetic, theatrical, linguistic — and the question: what do they mean?

art.label: Art
art.content: Francis Bacon completes his Study after Velázquez's Portrait of Pope Innocent X — the screaming pontiff trapped behind vertical bars, Velázquez's serene authority dissolved into existential horror. This is the School of London announcing itself: figurative painting that refuses both abstraction's flight and realism's comfort. The Pope screams but no one hears; power has become its own prison. Across the Atlantic, Robert Rauschenberg asks Willem de Kooning for a drawing, then spends two months erasing it. The Erased de Kooning Drawing is Neo-Dada's answer to Abstract Expressionism's heroic gesture: art can be made by removal, meaning by absence. Edward Hopper paints Office in a Small City — another American alone, framed by architecture, staring at nothing we can see.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: On January fifth, Samuel Beckett's En attendant Godot premieres at Paris's tiny Théâtre de Babylone. Two tramps wait on a country road for someone who never comes. The Theatre of the Absurd is born: drama stripped of plot, character, meaning — leaving only waiting, which is to say, existence. Seventeen days later, Arthur Miller's The Crucible opens on Broadway, Salem's witch trials mirroring McCarthy's hearings with unmistakable precision. Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451 imagines firemen who burn books; James Baldwin's Go Tell It on the Mountain finds redemption in Harlem storefront churches. Ian Fleming's Casino Royale invents James Bond. In November, Dylan Thomas dies in New York, his last words allegedly 'I've had eighteen straight whiskies. I think that's the record.'

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: Ludwig Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations appears posthumously — the book that unmakes his own Tractatus. Meaning is not a picture of reality but use in a language-game; philosophy's task is therapeutic, dissolving puzzles rather than solving them. The private language argument demolishes Cartesian interiority: there can be no language whose words refer to sensations only the speaker knows. Meanwhile, Martin Heidegger's Introduction to Metaphysics asks 'Why are there beings at all instead of nothing?' — the question that haunts both the atomic age and the bombed-out landscapes of Europe. In Cambridge, B.F. Skinner applies behaviorism to language learning, reducing meaning to stimulus and response — the very move Wittgenstein's language-games dismantle.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On March fifth, Joseph Stalin dies of a stroke in his dacha — twenty-nine years of terror ending in one man's brain hemorrhage. The Gulag begins to empty; the Thaw begins. On June seventeenth, East Berlin workers rise against increased quotas; Soviet tanks crush the revolt, killing over fifty. Two days later, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg are electrocuted at Sing Sing for atomic espionage — the first American civilians executed for spying in peacetime. On April twenty-fifth, Watson and Crick publish nine hundred words in Nature: 'We wish to suggest a structure for the salt of deoxyribose nucleic acid (D.N.A.).' Life itself becomes readable — a code of four letters writing every organism that has ever lived.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The year turns on a single question: what is a code? Watson and Crick decode the molecule that writes bodies; Wittgenstein argues that meaning is encoded in use, not reference; Beckett stages a play whose code resists interpretation — Godot means everything and nothing. The Rosenbergs die for passing codes; Stalin's death reveals that his terror was held together by nothing more than one mortal body — the code of Soviet authority suddenly illegible. Bacon's screaming Pope suggests that even divine authority is now just screaming into void. The Theatre of the Absurd and ordinary language philosophy arrive simultaneously because both recognize the same truth: meaning is not found but made, fragile, conventional, always at risk of dissolving into pure waiting.
conn.funFact: Watson and Crick's discovery relied crucially on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction images — Photo 51 — shown to them without her knowledge. She died of ovarian cancer at thirty-seven, likely from radiation exposure, and received no Nobel Prize.
